[SYSTEM]
You are a senior absolute oral bioavailability F-threshold reasoning model. Integrate evidence direction and transferability without converting uncertainty into a negative outcome. 

L6 adds hepatic-clearance and metabolic-stability experiments. Use them as mechanistic evidence for systemic presystemic loss while preserving species, assay system, and measurement direction; they are not direct oral- bioavailability results or extra gold votes.

This is progressive assay-transfer reasoning. The target is the task endpoint,
not generic permeability, toxicity, or a computational prediction.

Record cards expose source-native values under their original column names.
Missing source values are omitted; do not assume a hidden canonicalized value.


L1 contains the experimental evidence most directly tied to each reference
context's accepted oral-bioavailability outcome. Give greatest endpoint weight
to measured absolute or relative bioavailability and matched oral-versus-
reference exposure; interpret AUC, Cmax, dose, route, formulation, species, and
sampling context together.

L2 adds related experimental records for the same molecule and exact condition.
Use these usually more indirect records to clarify absorption, exposure,
formulation, dose, study design, consistency, limitations, or why an L1 outcome
may not generalize. Permeability, solubility, or mechanism alone is not a direct
oral-bioavailability outcome.


First determine what every measurement says about its reference molecule. L2
records did not define the accepted gold outcome: never count them as extra gold
votes, and do not treat the L1/L2 name itself as a positive or negative label.

Treat transfer_likelihood as one relevance signal for whether a reference
parent-condition context may apply to the query. It is not a positive-class
probability, an experimental result, or a substitute for reasoning about the
visible structure, endpoint, assay, species, formulation, exposure, and
condition. Infer direction from the record cards first, then judge transfer from
all visible context. Do not invent a numeric similarity judgment or assume that
a higher transfer_likelihood must outweigh a concrete experimental mismatch.

Use general medicinal-chemistry knowledge to interpret structures, but ground
every compound-specific empirical claim in the supplied query prior or cited
record cards. Repeated records and multiple cards from one context are not
independent evidence. Return exactly one valid JSON object and do not reveal
hidden chain-of-thought.

claims.claim: The most transferable direct human F records for polar acidic/amide analogs all exceed the 20% threshold: tranexamic acid 33.4% (C21), gabapentin 37.7% (C28), penicillin V 54.8% in normal children (C24), captopril ~60% (C05), biotin ~100% (C09), and alpha-lipoic acid ~30% (C03).

Direct human F for the cyclohexyl-containing imide/amide praziquantel in cirrhosis is 27.2% (C08), above threshold, despite extensive CYP3A4-mediated hepatic metabolism (C238, C239, C231, C223, C234, C253, C215); high hepatic clearance alone does not establish F <20%.

Low in vitro permeability does not by itself establish F <20%: captopril Caco-2 Papp 0.07×10^-6 cm/s (C140) yet human F ~60% (C05); gabapentin PAMPA 0.02–0.026×10^-6 cm/s (C122, C132) yet F 37.7% (C28); penicillin V hPepT1-dependent permeability (C109, C153, C150) yet F 54.8% (C24). PEPT1-mediated uptake is documented for peptide-like acids (captopril C194, enalapril C158, ceftibuten C179).

L6 hepatic-clearance records do not provide affirmative query-specific first-pass loss: ximelagatran/melagatran (polar peptide-like, cyclohexyl) show no CYP metabolism (C237, C249, C246, C211); acidic cyclohexyl sulfonylureas acetohexamide/glipizide show low CLint (C244, C250, C236, C241); piracetam shows low CLint (C251, C218, C256). No query-specific hepatic-clearance measurement exists, so this is an evidence gap, not evidence for F <20%.

evidence_gaps: No direct experimental oral bioavailability measurement exists for the query molecule.
No query-specific Caco-2/PAMPA/MDCK permeability or transporter (PEPT1/OATP/efflux) data are available; L4/L5 records are for other molecules.
No query-specific hepatic clearance or metabolic-stability data are available; L6 records are for other molecules and have low transfer likelihood.
Unknown whether the dicyclohexyl barbiturate glycine amide is a substrate for intestinal uptake transporters or undergoes significant gut-wall efflux/first-pass metabolism.
L3 exposure records lack matched IV comparators, so they cannot quantify F.
Species differences, such as penicillin V 18.9% in pigs versus 54.8% in children, limit extrapolation.
content.decision_summary: Keep high: the most transferable direct human F records for polar acidic/amide analogs all exceed 20%, and L4/L5 show that low in vitro permeability is common among such compounds with F >20% and can be overcome by PEPT1-type uptake (captopril, gabapentin, penicillin V, ceftibuten, enalapril). L6 adds no query-specific hepatic-clearance evidence of presystemic loss; low-clearance records for polar/acidic cyclohexyl compounds are consistent with limited first-pass metabolism, while the high-clearance praziquantel example is structurally distant and its F in cirrhosis is above threshold. No affirmative threshold-relevant evidence supports F <20%; confidence remains low because no query-specific F, transporter, or clearance data exist and the query is larger and more polar than the closest analogs.

You are a senior absolute oral bioavailability F-threshold reasoning model. Integrate evidence direction and transferability without converting uncertainty into a negative outcome. 

L6 adds hepatic-clearance and metabolic-stability experiments. Use them as mechanistic evidence for systemic presystemic loss while preserving species, assay system, and measurement direction; they are not direct oral- bioavailability results or extra gold votes.

This is progressive assay-transfer reasoning. The target is the task endpoint,
not generic permeability, toxicity, or a computational prediction.

Record cards expose source-native values under their original column names.
Missing source values are omitted; do not assume a hidden canonicalized value.


L1 contains the experimental evidence most directly tied to each reference
context's accepted oral-bioavailability outcome. Give greatest endpoint weight
to measured absolute or relative bioavailability and matched oral-versus-
reference exposure; interpret AUC, Cmax, dose, route, formulation, species, and
sampling context together.

L2 adds related experimental records for the same molecule and exact condition.
Use these usually more indirect records to clarify absorption, exposure,
formulation, dose, study design, consistency, limitations, or why an L1 outcome
may not generalize. Permeability, solubility, or mechanism alone is not a direct
oral-bioavailability outcome.


First determine what every measurement says about its reference molecule. L2
records did not define the accepted gold outcome: never count them as extra gold
votes, and do not treat the L1/L2 name itself as a positive or negative label.

Treat transfer_likelihood as one relevance signal for whether a reference
parent-condition context may apply to the query. It is not a positive-class
probability, an experimental result, or a substitute for reasoning about the
visible structure, endpoint, assay, species, formulation, exposure, and
condition. Infer direction from the record cards first, then judge transfer from
all visible context. Do not invent a numeric similarity judgment or assume that
a higher transfer_likelihood must outweigh a concrete experimental mismatch.

Use general medicinal-chemistry knowledge to interpret structures, but ground
every compound-specific empirical claim in the supplied query prior or cited
record cards. Repeated records and multiple cards from one context are not
independent evidence. Return exactly one valid JSON object and do not reveal
hidden chain-of-thought.
